verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, of [the] sons of Korah, upon alamoth, a song.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, from the sons of Korah, to be sung to the alamoth: a song.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a heading, not a verse of the song, and the Hebrew counts it as verse 1. That is why the KJV, which prints it unnumbered, is one number behind the Hebrew all the way down the psalm. It tells the performers three things: who leads (the choirmaster, the same title that opens 55 psalms), who owns the piece (the Levitical guild of the sons of Korah, who served in the temple choir, 1 Chr 6:31-37), and how to pitch it (על עלמות, 'on alamoth').

The KJV leaves 'Alamoth' untranslated, and rightly: nobody knows for sure. The word looks like 'maidens', so it may mean a high, women's or boys' register, or an instrument tuned to it. Rashi takes it as an instrument, citing 1 Chronicles 15:20, where lyres sit 'upon alamoth'. Play it as a high, bright voice over the opening, and then let it fall away.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'on / according to maidens'. Either a high voice or pitch, or an instrument of that kind; the tradition leans to a musical term. The same phrase appears in 1 Chr 15:20, in the list of Levitical musicians.
'For the one who leads / the choirmaster'. A participle of the verb נצח, which in the intensive stem means to oversee or conduct. The old rendering 'chief musician' is the same idea.

verses.translation_literal: God [is] to us a refuge and strength, a help in distresses, found exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: God is our shelter and our strength, a help in the narrow places, and to be found, always, close at hand.
verses.directors_commentary:
The whole psalm is one idea in three movements, and this is its thesis: before anything shakes, say where you stand. Start low and plain. Nobody in the choir is shouting; they are stating a fact they have tested.

Machaseh is the cleft in a rock where a hunted man hides from the storm, and ‘oz is strength. Tzarot, 'distresses', comes from a root meaning 'narrow' (tzar): the image is of being squeezed in a tight place with no room to move, which the KJV flattens to 'trouble'. The last two words are the surprise. Nimtza me'od is 'found, exceedingly'. The KJV's 'a very present help' keeps the sense, but it sounds like a stretched formula. The Hebrew is simpler and warmer: he is easy to find. Malbim hears three virtues here: a refuge, a help in need, and one you do not have to search for.

philological_notes.note: 'In distresses', from the root צרר 'to bind, press, be narrow'. The picture is being squeezed or hemmed in; the plural stresses repeated crises.

'Found exceedingly': a passive participle that means 'readily found / available'. The KJV 'very present' keeps the idea in one phrase. Metzudat David explains it as 'he is found to us always when we call'.

verses.translation_literal: Therefore we will not fear when the earth changes places, and when mountains shake in [the] heart of [the] seas.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so we will not be afraid, though the earth itself changes places beneath us, though the mountains stagger and sink into the very heart of the seas.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Therefore' ties this to verse 2: because he is found, we do not fear. Everything that follows is a list of the worst things the ancient mind could picture, and the singer rejects fear for each.

To an Israelite, the earth is a fixed platform and the mountains are its pillars; the sea is chaos held back by God's decree (Gen 1:9, Job 38:8-11). So 'the heart of the seas' is the deepest place there is, and a mountain falling into it is creation unmaking itself. Behamir ‘aretz is 'when the earth exchanges (itself)', a verb of swapping, and the KJV's 'be removed' loses that sense of the ground trading places. The KJV also smooths a rhythm: the Hebrew has two short, hard lines, not one long sentence.

Ibn Ezra and Radak hear a parable of wars and nations, Rashi hears the end of days; the stage direction is the same either way: the speaker stands still while the world moves.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive of the root מור 'to exchange, change'; here 'when [the earth] shifts / swaps place'. Metzudat Zion links it with תמורה 'exchange'.
'In the heart of the seas': the deep middle of the sea. Metzudat Zion explains that the sea has a 'heart' as the body does.

verses.translation_literal: Let its waters roar, let them foam; let [the] mountains quake at its swelling. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let its waters roar, let them churn to mud and foam; let the mountains tremble at its rising pride. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verbs are imperfects, so they can read as 'though they roar' (the KJV, which carries on from verse 3) or as the defiant 'let them roar': roar away. The two words, yehemu yechmeru, share an 'h-m' and a 'ch-m' and make the waves heard. The first is the noise of a crowd or a sea (hamah); the second is disputed, and the dispute is worth knowing. Rashi reads it as casting up mud, 'mud and mire and clay' as in Isaiah 57:20, from chomer 'clay'; Metzudat Zion ('from clay and mud') and Meiri ('mud and mire') agree, and Ibn Ezra's 'clouded like clay' is close. Rashi also records Menachem's different reading, which ties the verb to Lamentations 1:20, 'my bowels churn' (chamarmaru): to churn, be in turmoil. That reading supports the KJV's 'be troubled'. Both pictures fit a sea in a storm, one muddy, one boiling; the dramatic layer takes the mud, the literal layer stays at 'foam'.

Bega'avato is 'at its swelling' or 'in its pride', the word used of human arrogance, here given to the sea. Whose pride is it? On the plainest reading the suffix is the sea's; Rashi refers it to God, mentioned at the head of the psalm, which the grammar also allows. Selah is a marker we do not understand: a pause, a lift of the voice or an instrumental interlude. Let the choir hold one beat of silence.

philological_notes.note: Two readings. Rashi (with Metzudat Zion and Meiri) takes it from chomer 'clay, mud': the waters cast up mud and mire, as in Isa 57:20. Menachem, as Rashi reports, links it with Lam 1:20 (chamarmaru), 'churn, be in turmoil', which supports the KJV 'be troubled'. 'Foam' (STEPBible) is a neutral rendering of either.
'At its swelling / in its pride'. The word is usually used of human arrogance; here the sea is proud. Rashi refers the suffix to God, so the reading is open.
A liturgical marker of unknown meaning, most likely a pause, a lift or an interlude.

verses.translation_literal: A river: its streams make glad [the] city of God, [the] holy [place] of [the] dwellings of [the] Most High.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, quietly, a river. Its channels run bright and make the city of God glad, the holy ground where the Most High dwells.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns on one word. After the roaring sea, a river, with no verb and no warning: the sentence opens with the noun. Jerusalem has no river of its own. It sits above the Gihon spring and has the Siloam channel; the psalmist gives the city a river it never had, as Eden had one (Gen 2:10, which is what Rashi sees here), and as Ezekiel 47 and Joel 4:18 will give the temple. Against the sea's chaos, it is calm, living water.

Pelagav is 'its channels' or 'canals', small watercourses, a settled and tamed image. The verb yesamchu is an imperfect, which Hebrew leaves open between the present and the future: 'make glad' or 'shall make glad'. The KJV chose the future ('shall make glad'); the literal layer here takes the present, as the ASV does, because the psalm speaks of a standing fact. 'Ir elohim is 'city of God', and the KJV's 'tabernacles' for mishkenei is archaic: they are 'dwellings', the Most High's residence, and the plural may be a plural of majesty. The word 'elyon, 'Most High', was the title of a god in Canaan; here it names YHWH.

philological_notes.note: Intensive imperfect, 'they make glad'. An imperfect carries no fixed tense, so 'make glad' (present, as here) and 'shall make glad' (future, KJV) are both grammatical.
'Its channels / streams', from the root פלג 'to divide': water divided into watercourses. Metzudat Zion glosses it as an aqueduct or channel.
'Most High', from the root 'to go up'. An old divine title, found in the Abraham story (Gen 14:18-22) and in Canaanite religion; here an epithet of YHWH.

verses.translation_literal: God [is] in her midst; she will not be shaken. God will help her at [the] turning of morning.
verses.translation_dramatic: God is in her midst, and she will not be shaken. God will help her when the morning turns.
verses.directors_commentary:
The ground of the calm: God is inside the city. The same verb that was used of mountains in verse 3, moot, 'to shake', is used here of the city, and it is denied: the mountains may shake, she will not. The sound of the verse is the sound of that word: tamot, bal timmot.

The repeated 'God' is the hinge of the verse, and the KJV, which reads 'God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved: God shall help her, and that right early', turns the last words into an adverb. The Hebrew is a time, lifnot boker: literally 'at the turning of morning', the moment when darkness turns toward light. In a siege, the night watch ends at dawn and an attack comes then; Isaiah 37:36 has Jerusalem delivered at daybreak. Rashi takes it as the end of the redemption, Radak as the contrast between the evening of war and the morning of rescue. Say it as a promise, not a warning.

philological_notes.note: 'At the turning of the morning': the moment when morning turns, at first light. The KJV 'right early' is an interpretation. Ibn Ezra reads 'near the day, or every day'; Meiri compares 'when the day turns' (Jer 6:4).

verses.translation_literal: Nations roared; kingdoms shook. He gave with his voice; [the] earth melted.
verses.translation_dramatic: The nations roared; the kingdoms staggered. He lifted his voice, and the earth dissolved.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the sea of verse 3 becomes the nations. The same two verbs are used: hamu 'they roared' (as the water did in verse 4) and matu 'they shook' (as the mountains did in verse 3). The psalmist is telling you that the thing you feared in nature is the thing the empires do, and it is one single force that answers to one voice. Hamu goyim is the sound of a crowd: the same word is used of the noise of a city in the Rashi reference to 1 Kings 1:41.

The KJV 'the heathen raged' is a mistranslation of tone: goyim is 'nations', not specifically pagans, and the 'raging' is noise, not anger. 'He gave with his voice' is a deliberately odd phrase; the KJV smooths it into 'he uttered his voice'. And the earth does not tremble, it taMug: it melts like wax or dissolves, as in Exodus 15:15 where Canaan melts. Rashi cites that. The verbs are past tense, the prophet speaking of the future as already done (Metzudat David).

philological_notes.note: 'It melts / dissolves'. The root describes wax or snow giving way, and, as in Exod 15:15, a people's courage. Rashi lists this as 'melts', and cites the parallel.
'He gave with his voice': an idiom for raising the voice, 'he gave forth his voice'. The same idiom appears in Jer 12:8 and Ps 68:34.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH of hosts [is] with us; [the] God of Jacob [is] a high refuge for us. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our high refuge. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain, and the choir's loudest line so far. Two titles do the work. YHWH tzeva'ot, 'of hosts', is a war title: the armies of heaven, and of Israel, are his. The KJV 'Lord of hosts' hides the divine name behind 'Lord'; the Hebrew is the personal name. 'God of Jacob' is the humblest title for the God of a great one: Jacob, the trickster and the limping patriarch, who was also a fugitive, and whom the Most High did not leave.

Immanu, 'with us', is the heart of it: 'Immanuel', the name Isaiah gives (Isa 7:14), is built on this word. Misgav is a high place, a stronghold on a crag that the enemy cannot reach; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'strength'. The KJV renders both misgav here and machaseh in verse 2 as 'refuge', hiding that they are two different words; 'high tower' (YLT, BBE) is nearer, which is why the literal layer says 'a high refuge'. Ibn Ezra hears the nations seeing that God is with Israel, and so Israel does not fall as they do.

philological_notes.note: 'A high refuge, a stronghold': from the root שגב 'to be high, inaccessible'. A fortress on a height, not a shelter in a hollow, which is a different word (machaseh) in verse 2. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'strength'.
'YHWH of hosts': the divine name with a war title, 'armies' of heaven and earth. It is often read as the cult title of the Jerusalem temple.

verses.translation_literal: Go, see [the] works of YHWH, who has set desolations in the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Come, walk out and look at what the LORD has done: the ruins he has set in the land.
verses.directors_commentary:
A new voice, the voice of the guide, starts the second movement: a summons to see. Lekhu chazu is two imperatives, 'go, see', and the KJV's 'Come, behold' makes it a gentle invitation. In Hebrew it is an order to walk out to the scene, as one walks a battlefield afterward. Chazah is a seer's verb, 'to see a vision', not to glance.

The 'works' of YHWH are not creation but what he does to the armies. Shamot is 'desolations', the empty ruins left after a war, from the root of 'astonished, appalled'. The KJV's 'desolations' is right here. YLT's 'astonishing things' turns it to a miracle, and that is the root's other sense: a ruin so total it stops the passer-by. The verb sam, 'set, place', is the same one that sets a boundary or a monument: God has put these ruins down as one would put a sign.

philological_notes.note: 'Desolations, ruins'. From שמם 'to be desolate, appalled': the same root gives both a laid-waste place and the horror it causes. The KJV is right; YLT 'astonishing things' follows the second sense.

verses.translation_literal: Making wars cease to [the] end of the earth; [the] bow he breaks, and he cuts [the] spear in two; carts he burns with fire.
verses.translation_dramatic: He stops wars to the very edge of the earth; he snaps the bow, he cuts the spear in two, he sets the wagons burning in the fire.
verses.directors_commentary:
The guide names the works: an end to war. The first word is a participle, mashbit, 'one who makes cease', from the root of 'Sabbath': God makes war keep Sabbath. 'To the end of the earth' means the whole known world, and that matters, because the psalm began with local danger and has now become universal.

Three acts of destruction are drawn with precise verbs: the bow is broken (shiber), the spear cut through (kitzetz), the carts burned. All three are the equipment of an army, and burning captured war equipment is something Israel did (Josh 11:6, 9). The last noun is the one translators split on. Agalot is 'carts, wagons', the ordinary word for a baggage or farm cart; that is what the literal layer keeps. But the tradition reads it as war equipment: Rashi says 'war chariots' (rikhvei milchamot), Malbim 'the chariots in which he fights', and Metzudat David 'wagons made for war'. Ibn Ezra takes them as the carts that carry weapons or the soldiers' food, Meiri as carts bearing arms. The KJV, ASV and Webster's 'chariot' is therefore a supported interpretation, though not the plain meaning of the word, which is not the usual one for a war chariot (merkavah). The Targum has a different noun again, 'round shields'. Radak adds that the burning may be in anger or literal, like the fire and brimstone of Ezekiel 38. Whichever you choose, the stage picture is a pile of the army's gear in flames.

philological_notes.note: 'Carts, wagons', from עגל 'to roll'. Not the usual word for a war chariot (merkavah), but Rashi reads it as war chariots, Malbim as the chariots in which he fights, and Metzudat David as wagons made for war, so the KJV 'chariot' is an interpretation with support. Ibn Ezra takes them as wagons for weapons or provisions; the Targum has 'round shields'.
A causative participle, 'one who makes to cease'; the root שבת is that of Shabbat. Rashi glosses it as 'from us'; Metzudat Zion as 'cancels'.

verses.translation_literal: Let go, and know that I [am] God. I will be exalted among the nations; I will be exalted in the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let go. Drop your hands, and know that I am God. I will be raised high among the nations; I will be raised high over all the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The only verse in the psalm where God himself speaks, and the most misused. Harpu is a plural imperative and the order is to the nations, as Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak and Metzudat David all agree: the verb means 'let drop, slacken', and the picture is a soldier's hand letting go of a weapon (the same root as rafeh, 'limp, slack', in Jer 38:4 of the soldiers' hands). It is a command to surrender, not an invitation to inner peace. The KJV's 'Be still' is the source of the quiet-time reading, and the Hebrew does not support it: the speaker is God, the listeners are the armies, and the setting is a battlefield.

'Know' is the verb of recognition; they will have to admit it. The last half is a drumbeat: arum, 'I will be exalted', twice, once for the nations and once for the earth. Say it as a certainty, not a hope. The first-person pronoun anokhi, 'I', is the emphatic form, the one used at Sinai.

philological_notes.note: Plural imperative of the hiphil of רפה 'to sink, slacken': 'let go, drop, give up'. It is addressed to the nations in all the classical commentators. The KJV 'Be still' loses the military sense.
'I will be exalted, lifted up', repeated twice. A verb of rising, said of God's honor.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH of hosts [is] with us; [the] God of Jacob [is] a high refuge for us. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our high refuge. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain again, word for word, and the second time it must sound different. After God's own voice in verse 11, the choir answers him. The first time it was a claim made in the middle of a storm; now it is the response of people who have seen the bow broken. Radak hears Israel saying it after the rescue. Ibn Ezra adds that there is nothing left to fear since the wars have stopped; Meiri hears a prayer in the pangs before the end.

The KJV repeats 'Lord of hosts' and 'refuge' exactly as in verse 8, which keeps the refrain intact but hides, as there, that misgav is a 'high refuge' and not the machaseh of verse 2. The refrain stands after verses 8 and 12, so it closes the second and third movements of the psalm. Close the piece on the final Selah with a held silence.
